name: Average of 3
description: Computes the arithmetic mean of three values as (a+b+c)÷3. The result is the single value that, repeated three times, gives the same total.
notes: This is a simple unweighted mean of exactly three numbers; each value counts equally. For different weights, use a weighted average instead.

name: Percentage change
description: Computes the percentage change from an old value to a new value using (new−old)÷old×100. A positive result is an increase, a negative result a decrease.
notes: Change is relative to the old value, which must be nonzero. The sign shows direction; this differs from percentage-point change.

name: Weighted average (2)
description: Computes the weighted mean of two values as (v1×w1+v2×w2)÷(w1+w2), giving an average where each value contributes in proportion to its weight.
notes: Weights need not sum to any particular total; only their ratio matters. The sum of weights must be nonzero. Equal weights reduce to a plain average.

name: Range (max − min)
expression: max(a, b, c) - min(a, b, c)
description: Computes the statistical range of three values as the largest minus the smallest, max(a,b,c)−min(a,b,c). It measures how spread out the values are.
notes: The range uses only the extreme values, so it is sensitive to outliers and ignores the middle value. The result is never negative.

name: Z-score
description: Standardizes a value by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation, giving the z-score. It tells how many standard deviations the value lies above or below the mean.
notes: Standard deviation must be positive. A positive z is above the mean, negative below. Only comparable across distributions once standardized; it does not by itself give a probability.

name: Raw score from z-score
description: Reverses standardization by multiplying a z-score by the standard deviation and adding the mean, recovering the original raw value that corresponds to that z-score.
notes: This is the inverse of the z-score formula. A positive z returns a value above the mean; keep the same units and standard deviation used to compute the z-score.

name: Standard error of the mean
description: Divides the population standard deviation by the square root of the sample size to give the standard error of the mean, the typical spread of sample means around the true mean.
notes: Sample size n must be positive and larger n shrinks the error only as sqrt(n), so quadrupling n halves it. Uses the population sigma; with a sample std dev the same form applies as an estimate.

name: Margin of error
description: Multiplies a critical z-value by the standard error (sigma over root n) to give the margin of error for a mean. It is the half-width of the confidence interval around a sample mean.
notes: The z value sets the confidence level (1.96 for 95%). Assumes a known sigma and roughly normal sampling; for small samples with unknown sigma, use a t critical value instead.

name: Confidence interval upper bound
description: Adds the margin of error (z times sigma over root n) to the sample mean to give the upper limit of a confidence interval for the population mean.
notes: This gives only the upper bound; the lower bound subtracts the same margin. The z value fixes the confidence level (1.96 for 95%) and assumes an approximately normal sampling distribution.

name: Coefficient of variation
description: Divides the standard deviation by the mean and multiplies by 100 to give the coefficient of variation as a percentage, expressing relative variability independent of the unit of measurement.
notes: Meaningful only when the mean is positive and on a ratio scale with a true zero. It lets you compare dispersion across datasets with different units or very different means.

name: Mean of 2 values
description: Adds two values and divides by two to give their arithmetic mean, the simple average lying exactly midway between the two numbers.
notes: The result always falls between the two inputs. It weights both values equally; use a weighted average if they represent different sample sizes or importance.

name: Mean of 4 values
description: Sums four values and divides by four to give their arithmetic mean, the average value of the four numbers.
notes: All four values are weighted equally. The mean is sensitive to outliers, so a single extreme value can shift it noticeably.

name: Mean of 5 values
description: Sums five values and divides by five to give their arithmetic mean, the average of the five numbers.
notes: All five values are weighted equally. The mean is affected by outliers; consider the median if the data are skewed.

name: Weighted average of 3
description: Multiplies each of three values by its weight, sums the products, and divides by the total weight to give the weighted average, an average that counts each value in proportion to its weight.
notes: Total weight must not be zero. Weights need not sum to 1 since the division normalizes them; larger weights pull the result toward the corresponding value.

name: Population variance of 3 values
description: Computes the population variance of three values as the mean of the squared deviations from their average. It quantifies how far the three values spread from their mean.
notes: This divides by n (3), the population form; the sample variance divides by n − 1 instead. Units are the square of the input units, so take the square root for a comparable spread.

name: Population standard deviation of 3
description: Takes the square root of the population variance of three values, giving the population standard deviation, a measure of spread expressed in the same units as the data.
notes: This uses the population form dividing by n (3); the sample version divides by n − 1. Unlike variance, the result shares the units of the original values.

name: Normal distribution PDF
description: Evaluates the probability density of the normal (Gaussian) distribution at a point x given its mean and standard deviation. The result is the height of the bell curve at x, not a probability.
notes: Sigma must be positive. The output is a density, so it can exceed 1 for narrow distributions; probabilities come from the area under the curve, not from a single density value.

name: Probability complement
description: Subtracts a probability from one to give its complement, the probability that the event does not occur.
notes: The input p must lie between 0 and 1. It assumes exactly two outcomes (the event and its non-occurrence), which together account for all possibilities.

name: Independent AND probability
description: Multiplies two probabilities to give the chance that both independent events occur together (their intersection).
notes: Valid only when the events are independent; if one affects the other, use the conditional form p1 times P(2 given 1). Each probability must be between 0 and 1.

name: Independent OR probability
description: Uses the inclusion-exclusion rule to give the probability that at least one of two independent events occurs, adding the two probabilities and subtracting their joint probability.
notes: The subtracted term p1*p2 is the overlap, correct only when the events are independent. Omitting it double-counts the case where both occur; each probability must be between 0 and 1.

name: At least one occurrence
description: Computes the probability of at least one success in n independent trials as one minus the probability of no successes, where each trial succeeds with probability p.
notes: Assumes independent trials each with the same probability p. n should be a non-negative integer; the chance rises quickly toward 1 as trials accumulate.

name: Odds to probability
description: Converts odds (favorable to unfavorable) into a probability by dividing the odds by one plus the odds. The result is the chance of the event on a 0-to-1 scale.
notes: Here odds o are given as a single ratio (e.g. 3 means 3:1 in favor). Odds must be non-negative; the result always falls between 0 and 1.

name: Probability to odds
description: Converts a probability into odds by dividing it by its complement, giving the ratio of the chance the event happens to the chance it does not.
notes: Probability p must be between 0 and 1 and strictly less than 1, since p = 1 makes the denominator zero. A result of 3 means odds of 3 to 1 in favor.

name: Binomial single term
description: Evaluates one term of the binomial distribution: the probability of exactly k successes in n trials, as the number of combinations times p^k times (1−p)^(n−k). It gives the likelihood of a specific number of successes.
notes: The combinations term nCk must be supplied separately here; p is between 0 and 1 and k must not exceed n. This is the probability of exactly k successes, not k or more.

name: Expected value of 2 outcomes
description: Multiplies each of two outcomes by its probability and sums them to give the expected value, the probability-weighted average payoff over the two possible results.
notes: The two probabilities should sum to 1 for a complete distribution. Outcomes may be negative; the expected value is a long-run average, not a value any single trial must take.

name: Percentile rank position
description: Estimates the rank position corresponding to a given percentile in an ordered list of n items, using p/100 times (n+1). It locates where the percentile falls among the ranked data.
notes: Percentile p is on a 0-to-100 scale. The result is often fractional, meaning the value lies between two data points and must be interpolated; several percentile conventions exist besides (n+1).

name: Geometric mean of 2
description: Takes the square root of the product of two values to give their geometric mean, the central value appropriate for quantities that combine multiplicatively, such as growth rates.
notes: Both values should be positive for a meaningful result. The geometric mean is always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean and suits ratios or rates better than sums.

name: Geometric mean of 3
description: Takes the cube root of the product of three values to give their geometric mean, the multiplicative central value of the three numbers.
notes: All three values should be positive. Like the two-value case, it is suited to averaging growth factors or ratios rather than additive quantities.

name: Harmonic mean of 2
description: Computes the harmonic mean of two values as twice their product divided by their sum. It is the appropriate average for rates, such as speeds over equal distances.
notes: Values should be positive and their sum non-zero. The harmonic mean is always the smallest of the three Pythagorean means and is dominated by the smaller value.

name: Root mean square of 2
description: Computes the root mean square of two values as the square root of the mean of their squares. The RMS gives a magnitude-based average that weights larger values more heavily.
notes: Because it squares the inputs, sign is ignored and the result is always non-negative and at least as large as the arithmetic mean of the magnitudes.

name: Pearson correlation from components
description: Computes the Pearson correlation coefficient from summary components: the sum of cross products divided by the square root of the product of the two sums of squares. It measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship.
notes: Inputs are the (mean-centered) sums of products and squares, not raw data. The result lies between −1 and +1; near 0 means little linear association, and it captures linear relationships only.

name: Standard error of a proportion
description: Computes the standard error of a sample proportion as the square root of p times (1−p) divided by the sample size. It gauges the sampling variability of an estimated proportion.
notes: Proportion p is between 0 and 1 and n must be positive. The standard error is largest at p = 0.5; the normal approximation needs a reasonably large n and not-too-extreme p.

name: Margin of error for a proportion
description: Multiplies a critical z-value by the standard error of a proportion to give the margin of error, the half-width of a confidence interval for a population proportion.
notes: The z value sets the confidence level (1.96 for 95%); p is between 0 and 1 and n positive. The margin is widest near p = 0.5 and relies on the normal approximation.

name: One-sample t-statistic
description: Computes the one-sample t-statistic as the difference between the sample mean and the hypothesized population mean, divided by the standard error (sample std dev over root n). It measures how far the sample mean deviates from the hypothesized value in standard-error units.
notes: Uses the sample standard deviation, so it follows a t-distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom. A p-value requires that distribution, and the test assumes roughly normal data.

name: Cohen's d effect size
description: Computes Cohen's d as the difference between two means divided by the pooled standard deviation. It expresses the size of the difference between groups in standard-deviation units, independent of sample size.
notes: Use a pooled (common) standard deviation for s. Rough benchmarks are 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large; the sign shows which mean is larger.

name: Bayes' theorem
description: Applies Bayes' theorem to compute the posterior probability P(A|B) from the likelihood P(B|A), the prior P(A), and the evidence P(B). It updates the belief in A after observing B.
notes: All inputs are probabilities between 0 and 1 and P(B) must be non-zero. With a rare prior, even a strong likelihood can yield a modest posterior, the base-rate effect.

name: Chebyshev's inequality bound
description: Computes 1/k² from Chebyshev's inequality, the maximum fraction of any distribution's data that can lie more than k standard deviations from the mean. It bounds the tail proportion for any distribution.
notes: Valid for k greater than 1 and any distribution with finite variance. It is an upper bound, often loose; at least 1 − 1/k² of the data lies within k standard deviations.

name: Combined mean of 2 groups
description: Computes the overall mean of two groups by weighting each group's mean by its size, summing, and dividing by the total count. It gives the pooled mean as if the two groups were merged.
notes: Weights are the group sizes, so the larger group influences the result more. Total size must be positive; averaging the two group means directly is wrong unless the groups are equal in size.

name: Binomial Mean
description: Computes the mean (expected number of successes) of a binomial distribution as n*p, where n is the number of independent trials and p the success probability per trial.
notes: p must be a probability between 0 and 1 and n a non-negative integer. It assumes identical, independent trials with a fixed success probability.

name: Binomial Variance
description: Computes the variance of a binomial distribution as n*p*(1-p), where n is the number of trials and p the success probability. Variance is largest when p is near 0.5.
notes: p must lie between 0 and 1 and n be a non-negative integer. The (1-p) factor is the failure probability; variance vanishes when p is 0 or 1.

name: Binomial Standard Deviation
description: Computes the standard deviation of a binomial distribution as sqrt(n*p*(1-p)), the square root of its variance. It measures the typical spread of the number of successes around the mean n*p.
notes: p must be between 0 and 1 and n a non-negative integer. The result is in the same units as the count of successes.

name: Normal Probability Density
description: Evaluates the probability density of a normal (Gaussian) distribution at x, given mean mu and standard deviation sigma, using the bell-curve formula 1/(sigma*sqrt(2*pi)) * exp(-(x-mu)^2/(2*sigma^2)). It gives the height of the curve, not a probability.
notes: sigma must be positive. The output is a density (height of the curve), so it can exceed 1 for small sigma; areas under the curve, not heights, give probabilities.

name: Continuity-Corrected z
description: Computes a continuity-corrected z-score, (x - 0.5 - mu)/sigma, used when approximating a discrete distribution with the normal distribution. The 0.5 adjustment accounts for treating a discrete count as a continuous range.
notes: This particular form subtracts 0.5, appropriate for a right-tail (at least x) probability; use plus 0.5 for a left-tail. mu and sigma are the mean and standard deviation of the approximating normal.

name: z for Sample Mean
description: Computes the z-statistic for a sample mean, (xbar - mu)/(sigma/sqrt(n)), measuring how many standard errors the sample mean xbar lies from the population mean mu. The denominator is the standard error of the mean.
notes: Uses the known population standard deviation sigma, not a sample estimate. It relies on the sampling distribution of the mean being approximately normal.

name: t-Statistic (One Sample)
description: Computes the one-sample t-statistic, (xbar - mu)/(s/sqrt(n)), testing whether a sample mean xbar differs from a hypothesized mean mu. It uses the sample standard deviation s in the standard error.
notes: Unlike the z-statistic it uses the sample standard deviation s, so it follows a t-distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom. Assumes an approximately normal population.

name: Chi-Square Term
description: Computes a single term of the chi-square statistic, (observed - expected)^2/expected, comparing an observed count with its expected count. Summing this term over all categories gives the chi-square test statistic.
notes: The expected count must be positive and is conventionally at least 5 for the test to be valid. This gives one term only; add the terms across all categories for the full statistic.

name: Pooled Standard Deviation
description: Computes the pooled standard deviation of two samples, sqrt(((n1-1)*s1^2 + (n2-1)*s2^2)/(n1+n2-2)), a weighted combination of the two sample standard deviations. It estimates a common spread assumed shared by both groups.
notes: It assumes the two populations have equal variances. Sample sizes n1 and n2 must each be at least 2 so the denominator n1+n2-2 stays positive.

name: Cohen's d
description: Computes Cohen's d, an effect size given by (m1 - m2)/sp, the difference between two group means divided by the pooled standard deviation sp. It expresses the gap between groups in standard-deviation units.
notes: sp is the pooled standard deviation and must be positive. Roughly, 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 are often read as small, medium and large effects; the sign shows which group is larger.

name: Standard Error of Proportion
description: Computes the standard error of a sample proportion, sqrt(p*(1-p)/n), where p is the observed proportion and n the sample size. It quantifies how much the sample proportion is expected to vary from sample to sample.
notes: p must be between 0 and 1. The normal approximation behind it works best when both n*p and n*(1-p) are reasonably large (commonly at least 5 or 10).

name: CI Half-Width for Proportion
description: Computes the half-width (margin of error) of a confidence interval for a proportion, z*sqrt(p*(1-p)/n), where z is the critical value, p the sample proportion and n the sample size. Adding and subtracting it from p gives the interval.
notes: z sets the confidence level (about 1.96 for 95 percent). p must be between 0 and 1, and the normal approximation requires a sufficiently large sample.

name: Sample Size for Proportion
description: Estimates the minimum sample size needed to estimate a population proportion at a given confidence level and precision. It multiplies z² by the expected variance p(1-p) and divides by the squared margin of error moe².
notes: Use p and moe as decimal fractions, not percents. Set p=0.5 for the most conservative (largest) sample size when p is unknown. Round the result up to a whole number.

name: Regression Slope
description: Computes the slope of the least-squares regression line by dividing the sum of cross-products Sxy by the sum of squared x-deviations Sxx. The slope indicates how much y changes per unit increase in x.
notes: Sxy and Sxx are sums of deviations from the means, not raw sums. Sxx must be positive; a slope near zero implies little linear relationship between x and y.

name: Regression Intercept
description: Computes the y-intercept of the least-squares regression line as the mean of y minus the slope times the mean of x. This ensures the fitted line passes through the point of means (x̄, ȳ).
notes: Requires the slope b to already be estimated. The intercept is the predicted y when x=0, which may lie outside the observed data range and lack real meaning.

name: Pearson Correlation r
description: Computes the Pearson correlation coefficient by dividing the covariance Sxy by the product of the standard deviations of x and y. The result measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship.
notes: The value ranges from -1 to +1; near 0 means weak linear association. Correlation does not imply causation and captures only linear, not curved, relationships.

name: Coefficient of Determination
description: Squares the correlation coefficient r to give R², the proportion of variance in the dependent variable explained by the linear model. A value of 0.72, for example, means 72% of the variation is explained.
notes: R² lies between 0 and 1 and is always non-negative even for negative r. It never decreases when predictors are added, so a high R² alone does not confirm a good model.

name: Covariance of Two Points
description: Computes the covariance of two data points by averaging the products of each point's deviations from the mean of x and mean of y. A positive result indicates x and y tend to move together.
notes: This divides by 2 (population form for two points), not n-1. With only two points the result is limited and mainly illustrative of how covariance is built.

name: Percentile Rank
description: Computes the percentile rank of a value as the count of scores below it plus half the count equal to it, divided by the total count n, expressed as a percentage. It shows the relative standing of a value in a dataset.
notes: Uses the midpoint convention for ties (half of equal scores counted). The result ranges from 0 to 100%; n must equal the total number of observations.

name: Interquartile Range (IQR)
description: Computes the interquartile range as the third quartile Q3 minus the first quartile Q1. The IQR is the spread of the middle 50% of the data and is a robust measure of dispersion.
notes: Q3 must be at least Q1, so the result is non-negative. Being based on quartiles, the IQR resists outliers, unlike the full range or standard deviation.

name: Geometric Mean (2 values)
description: Computes the geometric mean of two values as the square root of their product. It is the appropriate average for ratios, rates, or multiplicative quantities such as growth factors.
notes: Both values must be positive; a zero or negative input makes the result zero or undefined. The geometric mean is always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean.

name: Harmonic Mean (2 values)
description: Computes the harmonic mean of two values as 2 divided by the sum of their reciprocals. It is the correct average for rates such as speeds over equal distances.
notes: Both values must be nonzero and are typically positive. The harmonic mean is always the smallest of the harmonic, geometric, and arithmetic means for positive numbers.

name: Root Mean Square (3 values)
description: Computes the root mean square of three values as the square root of the average of their squares. The RMS gives the effective magnitude and is used for quantities like AC voltage or deviations.
notes: Because values are squared, signs do not affect the result, so RMS is always non-negative. It is always greater than or equal to the arithmetic mean of the magnitudes.

name: Pearson Median Skewness
description: Computes Pearson's second skewness coefficient as three times the difference between mean and median, divided by the standard deviation. It gauges the direction and degree of asymmetry in a distribution.
notes: A positive value indicates a right-skewed distribution and negative a left-skewed one; zero suggests symmetry. Requires s greater than zero and is sensitive to the median estimate.

name: z to Percentile (Logistic Approx)
description: Approximates the cumulative normal probability for a z-score using a logistic function with the scaling constant 1.702. It returns the fraction of a standard normal distribution below the given z.
notes: This is an approximation, not the exact normal CDF; error is small but grows in the tails. The result lies strictly between 0 and 1; z=0 gives exactly 0.5.

name: Odds Ratio
description: Computes the odds ratio from a 2×2 table as the cross-product (a·d)/(b·c). It compares the odds of an outcome in the exposed group versus the unexposed group.
notes: An odds ratio of 1 means no association; above 1 suggests higher odds with exposure. Zero cells make it undefined or zero; the odds ratio overstates risk when the outcome is common.

name: Relative Risk
description: Computes the relative risk as the ratio of the incidence in the exposed group a/(a+b) to the incidence in the unexposed group c/(c+d). It shows how many times more likely the outcome is with exposure.
notes: A value of 1 means no difference in risk; above 1 means increased risk with exposure. Requires cohort or prospective data; the unexposed incidence must be nonzero.

name: Sensitivity
description: Computes the sensitivity (true positive rate) of a diagnostic test as true positives divided by all actually positive cases (true positives plus false negatives). It measures how well the test detects the condition.
notes: The result ranges from 0 to 1; high sensitivity means few missed cases (few false negatives). Sensitivity alone ignores false positives, so read it alongside specificity.

name: Specificity
description: Computes the specificity (true negative rate) of a diagnostic test as true negatives divided by all actually negative cases (true negatives plus false positives). It measures how well the test rules out the condition.
notes: The result ranges from 0 to 1; high specificity means few false alarms (few false positives). It complements sensitivity and should be interpreted together with it.

name: Prevalence
description: Computes prevalence as the number of diseased individuals divided by the total population size. It gives the proportion of a population that has the condition at a given time.
notes: The result is a fraction between 0 and 1; multiply by 100 for a percentage. Prevalence reflects existing cases, unlike incidence which counts new cases over time.

name: Expected Value (3 outcomes)
description: Computes the expected value of a discrete random variable with three outcomes as the sum of each outcome multiplied by its probability. It gives the long-run average value.
notes: The three probabilities should sum to 1 for a valid distribution and each lie between 0 and 1. Enter probabilities as decimals, not percents.

name: Sample Variance from Sum of Squares
description: Computes the sample variance using the computational form: the sum of squared values minus n times the squared mean, divided by n-1. It measures the spread of the data around the mean.
notes: Uses the n-1 (Bessel) divisor for an unbiased sample estimate, so n must be at least 2. Rounding error in sumsq or the mean can make small variances inaccurate.

name: SE of Difference of Two Means
description: Computes the standard error of the difference between two independent sample means as the square root of s1²/n1 plus s2²/n2. It quantifies the sampling variability of the mean difference.
notes: Assumes the two samples are independent; this unpooled form does not require equal variances. Enter s1 and s2 as standard deviations, not variances.

name: Pooled Proportion
description: Computes the pooled sample proportion by combining the successes from two groups (x1+x2) and dividing by the combined sample sizes (n1+n2). It is used as the common proportion in two-proportion tests.
notes: Used under the null hypothesis that both groups share the same proportion. x1 and x2 are counts of successes, not proportions; the result lies between 0 and 1.

name: Two-Proportion z-Statistic
description: Computes the z-statistic for comparing two sample proportions by dividing their difference by the pooled standard error, which uses the pooled proportion and both sample sizes. It tests whether the two proportions differ.
notes: Enter proportions and the pooled proportion as decimals. The test relies on a large-sample normal approximation and independent groups; compare the result to normal critical values.

name: F-Statistic (Variance Ratio)
description: Computes the F-statistic as the ratio of two sample variances, s1² divided by s2². It is used to test whether two populations have equal variances.
notes: Inputs are standard deviations and are squared internally to variances. Conventionally place the larger variance on top so F is at least 1; compare to F-distribution critical values.

name: Chebyshev Bound
description: Computes the minimum fraction of any distribution's data lying within k standard deviations of the mean as 1 minus 1/k². For k=2 it guarantees at least 75% of values fall in that range.
notes: Requires k greater than 1 to be meaningful. The bound holds for any distribution but is loose; actual proportions are usually much higher, especially for bell-shaped data.

name: Bayes Posterior Probability
description: Applies Bayes' theorem to compute the posterior probability of hypothesis A given evidence B, combining the likelihood P(B|A), the prior P(A), and the false-positive term P(B|not A)·P(not A). It updates belief after observing evidence.
notes: Enter all probabilities as decimals; P(A) and P(not A) should sum to 1. With a rare prior, even a high likelihood can yield a surprisingly low posterior (base-rate effect).

name: Precision (PPV)
description: Computes precision, or positive predictive value, as true positives divided by all predicted positives (true positives plus false positives). It gives the fraction of positive predictions that are correct.
notes: The result ranges from 0 to 1. Precision depends on prevalence, so a highly accurate test can still have low PPV when the condition is rare.

name: Negative Predictive Value
description: Computes the negative predictive value as true negatives divided by all predicted negatives (true negatives plus false negatives). It gives the fraction of negative predictions that are correct.
notes: The result ranges from 0 to 1 and, like PPV, depends on prevalence. A high NPV means a negative result is trustworthy for ruling out the condition.

name: Youden's J Index
description: Computes Youden's J index as sensitivity plus specificity minus 1, summarizing a diagnostic test's overall performance in a single number. It represents the maximum vertical distance from the ROC diagonal.
notes: The index ranges from 0 (useless) to 1 (perfect); it can be negative for a worse-than-chance test. It weights sensitivity and specificity equally regardless of prevalence.

name: Positive Likelihood Ratio
description: Computes the positive likelihood ratio as sensitivity divided by (1 minus specificity), i.e. the true positive rate over the false positive rate. It shows how much a positive test result raises the odds of disease.
notes: Values above 1 increase, and above 10 strongly increase, the probability of disease. The denominator (1 minus specificity) must be nonzero; a perfect specificity makes it undefined.

name: Accuracy
description: Computes classification accuracy as the number of correct predictions (true positives plus true negatives) divided by the total number of cases. It gives the overall fraction of correct classifications.
notes: The result ranges from 0 to 1. Accuracy can be misleading with imbalanced classes, where always predicting the majority class yields a high but uninformative value.

name: F1 Score
description: Computes the F1 score, the harmonic mean of precision and recall, as 2·TP divided by (2·TP + FP + FN). It balances precision and recall into a single measure of a classifier's performance.
notes: The result ranges from 0 to 1; being a harmonic mean, it is high only when both precision and recall are high. It ignores true negatives, so it suits imbalanced positive-focused tasks.

name: Exponential Distribution Mean
description: Computes the mean of an exponential distribution as the reciprocal of the rate parameter lambda. This mean is the average waiting time between events in a Poisson process.
notes: Lambda must be positive and is the number of events per unit time; the mean has the inverse unit (time per event). Do not confuse the rate with the mean itself.

name: Exponential Probability Density
description: Evaluates the exponential distribution's probability density function at x as lambda times e^(-lambda·x). It gives the relative likelihood of an event occurring at exactly time x.
notes: Defined for x greater than or equal to 0 with lambda positive; the density peaks at x=0 and decays. Density values are not probabilities and can exceed 1 when lambda is large.

name: Uniform Distribution Variance
description: Computes the variance of a continuous uniform distribution on the interval [a, b] as (b-a)² divided by 12. It measures the spread of values that are equally likely across the range.
notes: Requires b greater than a; the result depends only on the interval width, not its position. Take the square root to obtain the standard deviation.

name: Number Needed to Treat
description: Computes the number needed to treat as the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction (control event rate minus experimental event rate). It estimates how many patients must be treated to prevent one additional bad outcome.
notes: Enter event rates as decimals; the two rates must differ, and the control rate should exceed the experimental rate for a beneficial treatment. Round the result up to a whole number of patients.
